segments.heading: File comment: history of the versions, newest first
segments.text:
- The file starts with four history comments, one per version of the runner. This one describes the newest version: bwx12.c is the older runner bwx11.c plus 26 kernels and a third pad after them. No option and no output row is new.
- Every addition stands between a comment line `bwx12+` and a comment line `bwx12-`.
- The new kernels stand after the kernels of bwx11, in the source and in the kernel table. Lines 9 to 11 give the reason: the kernels of bwx11 keep their machine code and their loop offsets.
- Of the 26 new kernels the whole-chip test runs one: `read_nop256` (line 13).
- The third pad keeps the function `call` at the same start address modulo 64 as in bwx11. The build record (the file build.txt that the build script wrote on CRB) gives the start address 24 modulo 64 for both versions [Ref2].
- "Round 5" in line 3 names a round of work on the program. It is not a round of `--rounds`.

What bwx11 added to bwx10. The additions stand between `bwx11+` and `bwx11-`.
- 3 kernels: `read_nop64`, `read_nop96` and `read_nop128`. The whole-chip test runs `read_nop96`.
- A second pad after these kernels, again for the placement of `call`.
- The option `--evict-mb` and its output rows. They belong to the trial mode. The whole-chip test does not use the trial mode.

What bwx10 added to bwx8. The additions stand between `bwx10+` and `bwx10-`.
- 5 kernels: `read_pf256`, `read_pf512`, `read_pf1024`, `read_pf2048` and `read_1pl`. The whole-chip test runs `read_1pl`.
- The options `--rec-pad` and `--hot-copy`, and the output rows of lines 78 to 79. They belong to the trial mode.
- A pad after the new kernels, for the placement of `call`.

The oldest comment. bwx8.c is a copy of the first runner bwx.c, plus the trial mode.
- `--seq ...` names the interval mode. The comment says that its code is the text of bwx.c. `main` runs this mode when no argument is the word `--trial` (lines 2912 to 2914). The whole-chip test uses this mode only.
- `--trial` selects the trial mode. All its code stands after the function `parse_events` (after line 1793).
- Lines 98 to 99: the build uses the gcc flag `-fno-toplevel-reorder`. With it the kernels keep their place in the binary.
- Lines 101 to 103: on AArch64 the kernels are the real ones. On another machine a stand-in replaces every NEON kernel and every asm kernel, and the rates of such a build mean nothing. CRB ran the AArch64 build (see the row of line 491).
- Line 104: GB means 1e9 bytes in the whole file.

segments.heading: Includes and constants
segments.text:
- `_GNU_SOURCE` makes the Linux-specific declarations of the C library visible, for example `sched_setaffinity` and `CPU_SET`.
- `arm_neon.h` declares the NEON intrinsics. It is included only when the compiler builds for AArch64.
- `linux/perf_event.h` and `sys/syscall.h`: the structure `perf_event_attr` and the system call number for the counters (`open_counters`, line 1582).
- `pthread.h`, `sched.h` and `stdatomic.h`: threads and the barrier, CPU sets, and the atomic variables of the common start.
- `sys/mman.h`: `mmap`, `mprotect` and `madvise` for the buffers. `time.h`: `clock_gettime`.
- `setjmp.h` and `signal.h`: no line of bwx12.c itself uses them. The self-test file that line 2900 includes uses them.

- `HUGE_BYTES`: 2097152 bytes (2 MiB), the size of one 2 MiB page. Every buffer starts at a multiple of it.
- `MAX_CPUS`: the `--cpus` list may hold at most 1024 CPUs.
- `MAX_SEQ`: the `--seq` list may hold at most 64 kernels. The test uses 5 or 3.
- `MAX_EV`: the `--events` list may hold at most 8 events. The test uses 6.

- `CHECK_BYTES`: 8388608 bytes (8 MiB). Only `--stop pass` (line 1704) and the trial mode (line 2248) use it. The test runs with `--stop common`. So this value is not used in the test.
- `CHUNK_BYTES`: 2097152 bytes (2 MiB), the size of a chunk. With `--stop common` a worker calls the kernel on one chunk and then reads the clock (lines 1693 to 1700).
- `LEAD_NS`: 2000000 ns (2 ms). The main thread reads the clock and sets the common start of an interval to that clock value plus 2 ms (line 3059).
- `LATE_NS`: 100000 ns (100 us, which is 0.1 ms). A thread gets the late flag when its start clock read is more than this after the common start (line 1725).

`MAX_USE_CPU` is the highest CPU number that the process may use: 119, unless the build gives `-DMAX_USE_CPU=N`. The CRB build gave no `-D` option [Ref2]. `restrict_cpus` (line 368) and `parse_cpus` (line 388) apply the limit. The comment gives the rule of the test machine: CPUs 0 to 119 only, never 126 or 127.

segments.heading: Loop placement: the macro `PLACE` and the pads
segments.text:
- Aim: the loop of each kernel starts at a known address modulo 64 (the loop offset). The specification of the first runner treats this offset as a test factor [Ref10].
- `PLACE(name)` stands directly before the kernel `k_<name>`. It makes the function start at the address `PAD_<name>` modulo 64.
- `LOOP` is the planned loop offset. `HEAD` is the number of bytes from the function start to the loop start. `PAD` is `LOOP` minus `HEAD`, modulo 64.
- A kernel without a planned loop offset gets as `PAD` the start offset that its function has in bw_new or in bw_old (lines 157 to 159).
- Result in the CRB binary: the loop of `k_read` starts at 36 modulo 64, and the loop of `k_oldread` starts at 40 modulo 64 [Ref1].
- The `k_read` loop of bw_new also starts at 36 modulo 64, and the `k_read` loop of bw_old at 40 modulo 64 [Ref7]. So each of the two read kernels has the same loop offset in bwx12 as in its binary of part A.
`STR(x)` turns the value of the macro `x` into a text in quotes. Two steps are needed. `STR` first replaces a name such as `PAD_read` by its value 32. `STR2` then puts the quotes around the value.

- An `__asm__` statement outside of a function passes its text to the assembler without a change.
- `.pushsection .text`: continue in the code section of the program. `.popsection`: return to the section that was in use before.
- `.p2align 6`: fill up to the next address that is a multiple of 64 (2^6).
- `.fill N, 1, 0`: add N bytes with the value 0. N is the value of `PAD_<name>`.
- The comment of lines 145 to 146 names two gcc flags that this method needs: `-fno-toplevel-reorder` and `-falign-functions=4`. It adds that a pad must be a multiple of 4. Both flags are in the build record of CRB [Ref2].
- `-fno-toplevel-reorder`: the comment of lines 98 to 99 says that with this flag the kernels keep their place in the binary.
`PADOF(loop, head)`: `loop` minus `head`, modulo 64. The operation `& 63` keeps the low 6 bits. So a negative difference also gives a value from 0 to 63.

Planned loop offsets of the copy kernels: 36 for `copy`, 52 for `asmcopy` and for the three `asmcopy_c` kernels. A build with `-DB3_OFFSET=N` would use N for `copy` and `asmcopy`. The CRB build gave no `-D` option [Ref2]. The whole-chip test runs no copy kernel.

`HEAD` values of the copy kernels: 4 B or 20 B from the function start to the loop start. Each `#ifndef` block sets a default value that a `-D` option of the build can replace. The same pattern is used for every value up to line 251.

Pads of the copy kernels, computed with `PADOF`: 32 B for `copy`, `asmcopy`, `asmcopy2` and `asmcopy_c_reg`, and 48 B for `asmcopy_c` and `asmcopy_c_add`. The whole-chip test of 2026-11-17 runs none of these kernels.

Pads of three functions that run in the test.
- `PAD_read` = 32: the new read kernel `k_read` starts at 32 modulo 64. In the CRB binary it starts at the address 0x49a0, which is 32 modulo 64 [Ref1].
- `PAD_write` = 0: `k_write`, the function of the first touch, starts at 0 modulo 64. In the CRB binary it starts at 0x4a00 [Ref1].
- `PAD_asmread` = 0: `k_asmread` starts at 0 modulo 64. In the CRB binary it starts at 0x4ac0 [Ref1].
Pads of `asmread2` (0 B, the pad of `asmread`), `asmwrite` (32 B) and `asmwrite2` (32 B). The whole-chip test of 2026-11-17 runs none of these three kernels.
`PAD_oldread` = 0: the old read kernel `k_oldread` starts at 0 modulo 64. In the CRB binary it starts at the address 0x4600 [Ref1].
Pads of `oldread2` (0 B, the pad of `oldread`), `oldwrite` (32 B) and `oldcopy` (32 B). The whole-chip test of 2026-11-17 runs none of these three kernels.

Pads of `read_nop4`, `read_nop8`, `read_nop16`, `read_nop32` and `read_sparse`. All five use the pad of `asmread`, which is 0 B. The whole-chip test of 2026-11-17 runs none of them. The pads of the test kernels `read_1pl`, `read_nop96` and `read_nop256` are defined later in the file (lines 927 to 929, 1056 to 1058 and 1134 to 1136).

segments.heading: Data types and global variables
segments.text:
- `enum ktype`: the four kernel types. The function `call` (line 1491) chooses the argument list of a kernel by its type.
- `read_fn` (type T_READ): the kernel gets the start address and the number of 8-byte words. It returns nothing. The test kernels `read`, `asmread`, `read_nop96`, `read_nop256` and `read_1pl` have this type.
- `oldread_fn` (type T_OLDREAD): the same two arguments, and the kernel returns a 64-bit sum. The test kernel `oldread` has this type.
- `write_fn` and `copy_fn`: the types of the write kernels and the copy kernels. No timed interval of the test runs a kernel of these two types.

One entry of the `--seq` list: the index of the kernel in the kernel table, and the size of the range that the kernel works on. `bytes` is 0 when the entry has no `@SIZE` part. `main` then sets it to the `--bytes` value (lines 2989 to 2990). In the test every entry gets 268435456 bytes (256 MiB).

`cfg` holds the settings of the process. Values in the test:
- `threads` = 120. `ncpus` = 120, and `cpus[i]` = i for i from 0 to 119.
- `bytes` = 268435456 (256 MiB per thread).
- `min_s` = 6.0: the deadline of an interval is 6 s after its common start.
- `use_thp` = 1: the program asks for 2 MiB pages.
- `seq` and `nseq`: the kernel list of `--seq`. It has 5 entries for like.spec and 3 entries for cfwd.spec and crev.spec. `rounds` = 2: the list runs 2 times.

- `stop_common` = 1 (`--stop common`).
- `start_offset` = 0 (`--start common`): every thread starts each interval at byte 0 of its own buffer (line 1662). This option chooses a place in the buffer. It does not set the start time of an interval.
- `two_buffers` = 0: no copy kernel is in the list, and each thread has one buffer.
- `count` = 1 (`--count`). `pmu_type` = 11. `nev` = 6, with the 6 names and the 6 codes of `--events`.
- Line 282 sets the defaults: 1 thread, 0.5 s per interval, a request for 2 MiB pages, 1 round, and no PMU type (-1). Every other field starts at 0.

The page state of one buffer: its size and the part of it on 2 MiB pages, both in kB. `read_smaps` (line 1515) fills it. The value -1 means that the buffer was not found as one exact entry of `/proc/self/smaps`. It is printed as `NA`.
One reading of the counters of a thread: the thread CPU time, the enabled time and the running time of the counter group, and one value per event.

The result of one thread for one interval.
- `bytes`: the bytes that the thread counted in the interval. `late`: the late flag.
- `t_sched`: the common start time. `t_start`: the start clock read `t0` of the thread. `t_end`: its last clock read `t1`. All three are values of the clock CLOCK_MONOTONIC in ns.
- `c0` and `c1`: the counter readings before `t0` and after the last `t1`.
- `pg` and `vm`: only a process with one thread uses them. The test does not.
- The worker stores the structure at line 1726, before its barrier of line 1727. `main` reads it after its barrier of line 3064. So the two threads never use it at the same time.

One record per worker.
- `idx`: the thread number, 0 to 119 in the test. `cpu`: the CPU of the thread. In the test the two are equal (line 3011).
- `a`: the buffer. `b`: the second buffer, which only a copy kernel needs. It stays NULL in the test.
- `group_fd`, `ev_pos` and `nopen`: the counter group of the thread. `open_counters` (line 1582) sets them.
- `res`: the result of the last interval. `tid`: the thread handle that `pthread_create` returns.

- `bar`: the barrier. `main` creates it for 121 threads at line 3005.
- `t_base_ns`: the clock value at the process start (line 2908). The times in the T rows are relative to it.
- `page_bytes`: the page size that Linux reports (line 2909). `alloc_buf` uses it.

The three shared variables of the common start. `_Atomic`: every load and every store of such a variable is one indivisible step.
- `gen` starts at 0 and only grows.
- For each interval `main` first stores the start time `t_sched_ns` and the stop time `deadline_ns`. Then it adds 1 to `gen` (lines 3060 to 3062).
- A worker first waits for the new value of `gen` (line 1677). Then it loads the two times (lines 1679 to 1680). So it never uses the times of the interval before.

segments.heading: Function `now_ns`: the clock
segments.text:
Reads the Linux clock CLOCK_MONOTONIC with `clock_gettime` and returns the time in ns as one 64-bit number. Every time stamp of the program comes from this function.
- In a timed interval the worker calls it once for the start `t0` (line 1688) and once after each 2 MiB chunk for `t1` (line 1700).
- So one clock read per chunk is inside the timed interval. This is the same for every kernel of the test.

segments.heading: Function `parse_bytes`: a size text such as `256M`
segments.text: `strtod` reads the number. A letter after it multiplies the number: `k` or `K` by 2^10, `m` or `M` by 2^20, `g` or `G` by 2^30. In the test `--bytes 256M` gives 256 times 2^20, which is 268435456 bytes. `main` calls the function for `--bytes` (line 2937).

The program ends with the message `bad size` and exit status 2 in four cases: the text holds no number, other text follows the size, the value is 0 or below, or the size is 0 bytes after rounding. Otherwise the function returns the size in bytes.

segments.heading: Function `parse_long`: a whole number inside a range
segments.text: `strtol` reads a decimal whole number. The program ends with exit status 2 when the text holds no digit, when other text follows the number, when the number does not fit the type `long`, or when it lies outside the range `lo` to `hi`. On the path of the test: `--threads 120` (allowed 1 to 4096), `--rounds 2` (1 to 1000000) and `--pmu-type 11` (0 to 2147483647).

segments.heading: Function `restrict_cpus`: no CPU above 119
segments.text:
- `sched_getaffinity` reads the set of CPUs on which Linux may run the calling thread. The first argument 0 means the calling thread. A failure ends the program with exit status 2.
- `main` calls this function before it creates a thread (line 2911). The comment says that the main thread and every worker then stay on the permitted CPUs.
Removes every CPU number above `MAX_USE_CPU` (119) from the set. `changed` records whether the set held such a CPU. `CPU_SETSIZE` is the number of CPUs that the set type of the C library can hold.

- Only when a CPU was removed, `sched_setaffinity` passes the smaller set to Linux. An empty set or a failed call ends the program with exit status 2.
- In the test the script rx.sh starts the program under `taskset -c 0-119` [Ref3]. So the set holds no CPU above 119, `changed` stays 0, and the function changes nothing.

segments.heading: Function `parse_cpus`: the value of `--cpus`
segments.text:
- `strtok` splits the list at each comma. The loop handles one item per pass.
- An item is one number, a range `lo-hi`, or a range with a step `lo-hi:step`. `strtol` reads each number.
- When no digit follows `-` or `:`, lines 395 and 398 set `e` back to `tok`. The test of line 401 then rejects the item.
- In the test the list is `0-63,64-119`: two ranges with the step 1.
Rejects an item that holds other text, a negative start, an end below the start, an end above 119 (`MAX_USE_CPU`), or a step below 1. The program then ends with exit status 2.

- Appends every CPU number of the item to `cfg.cpus` and counts it in `cfg.ncpus`. More than 1024 entries end the program with exit status 2.
- In the test the result is 120 entries in rising order: `cfg.cpus[i]` = i.
- `main` gives thread i the CPU `cfg.cpus[i]` (line 3011). So the threads 0 to 63 get the CPUs of mesh 0, and the threads 64 to 119 get CPUs of mesh 1.

segments.heading: Function `pin_cpu`: bind the calling thread to one CPU
segments.text:
- Builds a CPU set that holds only `cpu` and passes it to `sched_setaffinity`. The first argument 0 means the calling thread.
- After the call Linux runs this thread on that CPU only.
- A failure ends the program with exit status 2.
- Each worker calls the function at its start (line 1642), before it opens its counters and before it maps its buffer.

segments.heading: Function `buf_len`: the length of one buffer
segments.text: Rounds the `--bytes` value up to a multiple of 2 MiB. In the test the value 268435456 is already 128 times 2 MiB. So the result is 268435456 bytes.

segments.heading: Function `alloc_buf`: map one buffer, aligned to 2 MiB
segments.text:
- Each worker calls this function once, after it has pinned itself (line 1645).
- `len` is the buffer length: 268435456 bytes (256 MiB) in the test.
- `maplen` is 4 MiB more: 272629760 bytes (260 MiB). The extra 4 MiB are needed for the alignment of line 442 and for the two no-access ranges of lines 443 to 444.

- `mmap` asks Linux for `maplen` bytes of new memory that the process may read and write.
- `MAP_PRIVATE | MAP_ANONYMOUS`: the memory belongs to this process only, and no file backs it. `NULL`: Linux chooses the address.
- A failed `mmap` ends the program with exit status 2.
- The call does not yet give physical memory to the pages. That happens at the first touch (line 1646).

`p` is the buffer start: the first 2 MiB boundary that lies at least one page above the start `raw` of the mapping. `page_bytes` is the page size of Linux. The buffer is the range from `p` to `p + len`. So it starts at an address that is a multiple of 2 MiB.

- `mprotect` with `PROT_NONE` forbids every access to the unused range before the buffer and to the unused range after it.
- The comment of lines 431 to 433 gives the purpose: the buffer is then one entry of its own in `/proc/self/smaps`. `read_smaps` (line 1515) looks for an entry with exactly the start and the end of the buffer.
- A failed `mprotect` only prints a message, and the run continues. The script rx.sh writes the error output of the program to the file stderr.txt [Ref3]. In the test every stderr.txt is empty [Ref5].

- `madvise` with `MADV_HUGEPAGE` asks Linux to use 2 MiB pages for the buffer.
- `cfg.use_thp` is 1 in the test. Only the option `--no-thp` sets it to 0 (line 2926), and no argument line of the test holds this option [Ref4].
- A failed `madvise` only prints a message, and the run continues.
- This function does not test whether the buffer got 2 MiB pages. The P rows show it: in the test each P row reports 262144 kB of 262144 kB on 2 MiB pages [Ref5].
Returns the buffer start as a pointer to 8-byte words. No code of the interval mode unmaps a buffer. The buffer stays mapped until the process ends.

segments.heading: Old kernels: code of the old benchmark source
segments.text:
- The comment says: the kernels below are `k_read`, `k_write` and `k_copy` of bandwidth.orig.c, the benchmark source until 2026-11-13, under new names.
- So `oldread` is the old read kernel. Apart from absolute addresses, its machine code in bwx12 has the same instruction text as `k_read` of the binary bw_old [Ref7].
- The quoted old comment gives the reason for the 16 running sums ("accumulators"): with 16 separate sums the adds should not limit the speed of the loop. This is a statement of the old comment. It is not a result of the whole-chip test.
- The old comment expects that gcc keeps the 16 sums in 8 vector registers. The machine-code listing of the CRB binary confirms it: the sums are in the registers v24 to v31 [Ref1].
- `oldread2` is the A/A copy. Line 459: the build uses the gcc flag `-fno-ipa-icf`, and gcc then keeps both functions. The flag is in the build record [Ref2].

segments.heading: Macro `DEF_OLDREAD`: source text of the old read kernel
segments.text:
- `DEF_OLDREAD(name)` writes `PLACE(name)` and one function `k_<name>`.
- `a` is the start of the range to read. `n` is the length of the range in 8-byte words. The function returns a 64-bit sum.
- `noinline`: gcc must keep the function separate from its caller. The listing shows `k_oldread` as a function of its own [Ref1].
- In a timed interval of the test one call gets one 2 MiB chunk: `n` = 262144 words (line 1695). The warm-up pass calls the kernel once on the whole buffer (line 1669).

`s` holds the 16 running sums. All start at 0. Machine code, once per call and before the loop [Ref1]: 4 `stp` instructions (each stores two 16-byte registers) write 128 B of zeros to the stack, and the 8 registers v24 to v31 are set to 0. During the loop these 8 registers hold the 16 sums, two sums per register.

- Source: the outer loop takes 16 words (128 B) per pass. The inner loop adds word `j` of these 16 words to sum `j`. So every loaded word is an input of one add.
- Machine code: gcc compiled the inner loop to vector instructions. One loop pass is 16 instructions for 128 B [Ref1].
- 4 `ldp q` loads of 32 B each, at the byte offsets 0, 32, 64 and 96 from the read position.
- 8 vector adds. Each one adds one loaded register to one of the sum registers v24 to v31. One vector add performs two of the 16 adds of the source.
- `add x0, x0, #0x80` moves the read position by 128 B. `add x1, x1, #0x1` counts the pass. `cmp` and `b.cc` branch back while the count is below the number of passes.
- No instruction of the loop stores to memory. gcc did not unroll the loop: one pass of the machine loop is one pass of the outer source loop.

- After the loop the function adds the 16 sums into one value and returns it.
- Machine code, once per call [Ref1]: the 8 sum registers are stored to the stack and loaded back. Then 7 vector adds and one `addp` add them into one number. `addp` adds the two 64-bit halves of one register. `fmov x0, d31` copies the result into the return register x0.
- `call` stores the returned value into the volatile variable `sink` (line 1500). So the sum is used, and the compiler cannot remove the loads and the adds as unused work.
- gcc also added a stack check to this function. It saves a guard value on the stack at the start and compares it before the return. A changed value leads to a call of `__stack_chk_fail` [Ref1].
- One call runs 53 instructions outside the loop. One 2 MiB chunk is 16384 loop passes, which are 262144 instructions.

segments.heading: Function `k_oldread`: kernel `oldread`, the old read kernel
segments.text:
- This line creates the function `k_oldread`. It is the kernel `oldread` of `--seq`, with the type T_OLDREAD in the kernel table (line 1462).
- In the CRB binary the function starts at the address 0x4600 and its loop at 0x4668 (40 modulo 64) [Ref1].
- For 256 B it runs 2 loop passes: 32 instructions with 8 `ldp q` loads, 16 vector adds and 2 branches. The new read kernel runs 11 instructions for 256 B (see the row of line 527).

segments.heading: Function `k_oldread2`: A/A copy, not run in the test
segments.text: Creates `k_oldread2`, the A/A copy of the old read kernel. The whole-chip test of 2026-11-17 does not run it.

segments.heading: Function `k_oldwrite`: old write kernel, not run in the test
segments.text: The kernel `oldwrite`: a plain C loop that stores the value `v` to every 8-byte word of the range. The whole-chip test of 2026-11-17 does not run it. The first touch of a buffer uses `k_write` (line 531).

segments.heading: Function `k_oldcopy`: old copy kernel, not run in the test
segments.text: The kernel `oldcopy`: a plain C loop that copies `n` 8-byte words from `s` to `d`. `restrict` tells the compiler that the two ranges do not overlap. The whole-chip test of 2026-11-17 does not run it.

segments.heading: AArch64 branch: the kernels of the CRB binary
segments.text:
- `#if defined(__aarch64__)`: the lines from here to the `#else` of line 851 are compiled only for AArch64. The lines from that `#else` to the `#endif` of line 897 hold the stand-ins for other machines.
- The CRB binary was compiled from this first branch, and `STANDIN` is 0. Proof: line 3024 prints `kernels=aarch64` only in this case, and line 2 of every csv file of the test holds this text [Ref5].
- Comment: the C kernels below are unchanged from the benchmark source bandwidth.c. Each loop pass moves 256 B as 16 vectors of 16 B and does no arithmetic on the data.
- The caller must pass a size that is a multiple of 256 B and not 0. `main` checks the sizes (lines 2973 and 2991). A chunk is 2 MiB.

segments.heading: Function `k_read`: kernel `read`, the new read kernel
segments.text: `PLACE(read)` with `PAD_read` = 32: the function starts at 32 modulo 64. In the CRB binary `k_read` starts at the address 0x49a0 and its loop at 0x49a4 (36 modulo 64) [Ref1]. The loop of `k_read` in bw_new has the same offset 36 [Ref7].

- This is the kernel `read` of `--seq`, with the type T_READ in the kernel table (line 1460). In the test only part C runs it.
- `a` is the start of the range to read. `n` is the length of the range in 8-byte words. The function returns nothing: it computes no sum.
- `noinline`: gcc must keep the function separate from its caller. The listing shows it as a function of 13 instructions [Ref1].
- Apart from absolute addresses, its instruction text equals the text of `k_read` in bw_new, the binary of part A [Ref7].
- In a timed interval of the test one call gets one 2 MiB chunk: `n` = 262144 words (line 1695). The warm-up pass calls the kernel once on the whole buffer (line 1669).

- `p` is the read position. `end` is the first address after the range: `a` plus `n` words.
- Machine code, once per call and before the loop: `add x1, x0, x1, lsl #3` [Ref1].
- Before this instruction the register x0 holds `a` and x1 holds `n`. After it x1 holds `end`.
`do`: the loop body runs once before the first test of the end. So the range must not be empty.

- Each `vld1q_u64(p + k)` loads 16 B, which are two 8-byte words, from word `k` after the read position.
- These 4 lines load the bytes 0 to 63 of the current 256 B block.
- Machine code: gcc joined each two neighbour loads into one `ldp q` load of 32 B. For these 4 lines: `ldp q31, q30, [x0]` and `ldp q29, q28, [x0, #32]` [Ref1].
The loads of the bytes 64 to 127 of the block. Machine code: `ldp q27, q26, [x0, #64]` and `ldp q25, q24, [x0, #96]` [Ref1].
The loads of the bytes 128 to 191 of the block. Machine code: `ldp q23, q22, [x0, #128]` and `ldp q21, q20, [x0, #160]` [Ref1].
